Rectangular bronze ding (sacrificial vessel), one of the common types of Chinese ritual bronzes, of the ancient Chinese Shang dynasty; 12th century BC. Statement E55: Type
The heaviest piece of bronzeware to survive from anywhere in the ancient world; the largest and heaviest ancient Chinese bronzeware yet discovered; the only one of its kind in the world, and a representative work of Shang bronzeware. Statement E55: Type
Compared to earlier ding, such as the Duling fangdings, it is wider and its walls are thicker, making it much more massive. (The Duling fangdings are not modelled here; the comparison is recorded as a descriptive statement about this vessel.) Description E55: Type
The article records no condition state, no conservation report and no assessment of the vessel's state of preservation. Nothing is modelled for condition. Documentation gap E55: Type
The article records no reconstruction, restoration, repair or physical alteration of the vessel, whether current, later reversed or superseded. Nothing is modelled for alteration. What did change and was superseded is the vessel's name, which is modelled under identity. Documentation gap E55: Type
The article records no acquisition, no transfer of legal title, no purchase, no gift and no legal determination of ownership at any date. No instance of E8 Acquisition is modelled. Custody is asserted only to the extent the article supports it: the vessel is at the National Museum of China. Documentation gap E55: Type
The article records no depositional event for the vessel: no burial, no tomb, no stratigraphic context, no grave assemblage. It is said only to have been "unearthed". Tomb 260 at Yinxu, the tomb of Fu Jing, is mentioned but is NOT stated to be the vessel's findspot; the article in fact contrasts the two, the vessel having been found in 1939 at Wuguan Village and the tomb only located in 1959. No deposition is modelled. Documentation gap E55: Type

Chinese bronzeware naming convention E29: Design or Procedure The naming of bronzeware generally follows this principle: the last character is usually the type of the ware, e.g. ding, dou, hu, pan, or zun. Since this bronzeware is a ding, it is called XX ding. The specific type of ding depends on whether the ware has an inscription. If there is an inscription, the character in the inscription that can reflect the name of the owner of the ware is used as the name of the ding. 网易, 郭沫若：此鼎叫司母戊鼎，专家：是后母戊，郭沫若：你们会后悔的, 2020-06-23 E31: Document
